title: Wolstenholme Primes: Computational Number Theory at the Frontier
content: A Wolstenholme prime is a prime p where C(2p-1, p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p⁴), strengthening Wolstenholme's classical theorem (mod p³ for all p ≥ 5). Only two are known: 16843 (McIntosh 1995) and 2124679 (McIntosh-Roettger 2007). This formalization tackles the open question: both known Wolstenholme primes are ≡ 3 (mod 4) — is this a coincidence or a structural constraint? The file combines computational verification (native_decide for small primes and primality), axiomatized large computations (binomial coefficients too large for the kernel), and logical reasoning about the residue structure.
mathContext: Wolstenholme's theorem: $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^3}$ for all primes $p \geq 5$. Wolstenholme prime: a prime where the congruence holds $\pmod{p^4}$. Only $p = 16843$ and $p = 2124679$ are known, both $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.

title: Core Definitions: cb and IsWP
content: `cb p = Nat.choose (2*p-1) (p-1)` is the 'central-ish' binomial coefficient — not quite the central binomial coefficient C(2p,p) but related by C(2p,p) = 2·cb(p). `IsWP p` requires both primality and the mod p⁴ congruence cb(p) % p⁴ = 1. This definition separates the computational check (mod p⁴) from the primality requirement, allowing them to be verified independently.

title: Structural Properties: WPs Are Odd and At Least 5
content: Three structural facts. `wp_ge_five`: exhaustive case analysis on p ∈ {0,1,2,3,4} using `native_decide` (2,3 fail the mod p⁴ test) and `decide` (0,1,4 aren't prime). `wp_odd`: since the only even prime is 2 and WPs are ≥ 5, every WP is odd — proved by showing 2∣p contradicts primality for p ≥ 5. `wp_mod4_cases`: an odd number is either 1 or 3 mod 4, established by `omega` from wp_odd. This sets up the dichotomy: the open question asks which of these two residue classes actually contains Wolstenholme primes.
mathContext: Every WP $p \geq 5$ (computational exclusion of $p \leq 4$). Since $p$ is odd, $p \bmod 4 \in \{1, 3\}$. The open question: is $\{p : \text{IsWP}(p)\} \subseteq \{p : p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}\}$?

title: Computational Exclusion of Small Primes
content: Seven theorems proving primes 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 are NOT Wolstenholme primes. Each proof is identical: assume IsWP p, extract the mod p⁴ condition, and refute it with `native_decide`. This establishes a computational gap: the first WP is 16843, over 700× larger than 23. The pattern demonstrates that checking WP status is computationally feasible for small primes but becomes infeasible as the binomial coefficient grows super-exponentially.
mathContext: $\binom{9}{4} = 126$, $126 \bmod 625 = 126 \neq 1$ (p=5 fails). $\binom{13}{6} = 1716$, $1716 \bmod 2401 = 1716 \neq 1$ (p=7 fails). The kernel can evaluate these, but $\binom{33685}{16842}$ for $p=16843$ is astronomically large.

title: The Two Known Wolstenholme Primes
content: Primality of 16843 and 2124679 is verified computationally via `native_decide`. The mod p⁴ congruences are axiomatized because C(33685, 16842) and C(4249357, 2124678) are astronomical numbers exceeding the kernel's computation capacity. The axioms cite McIntosh-Roettger (2008). `isWP_16843` and `isWP_2124679` combine primality and the axioms into the IsWP witnesses. `exists_two_distinct_wp` provides the existential that at least two distinct WPs exist, with the distinctness witness `by omega`.
mathContext: $16843$ and $2124679$ are both prime (by `native_decide`). $\binom{33685}{16842} \equiv 1 \pmod{16843^4}$ and $\binom{4249357}{2124678} \equiv 1 \pmod{2124679^4}$ (axiomatized from McIntosh-Roettger 2008).

title: Residue Analysis: The Mod 4/8/12 Pattern
content: Both known WPs are ≡ 3 (mod 4), but they differ mod 8: 16843 ≡ 3 (mod 8) while 2124679 ≡ 7 (mod 8), covering both odd residue classes that map to 3 (mod 4). Intriguingly, both share residue 7 (mod 12). Whether the mod 12 coincidence reflects a structural constraint or is accidental is unknown — with only two data points, statistical inference is impossible. The `known_wp_all_mod4_eq_3` theorem packages the mod 4 observation as a single lemma over both known WPs using case analysis.
mathContext: Mod 4: $16843 \equiv 2124679 \equiv 3$. Mod 8: $16843 \equiv 3$, $2124679 \equiv 7$. Mod 12: $16843 \equiv 2124679 \equiv 7$. The mod 8 data rules out a mod-8 pattern, but the mod 4 and mod 12 patterns are unexplained.

title: The Open Question and Logical Equivalence
content: `WPMod1Exists` and `AllWPMod3` formalize the two sides of the dichotomy. The key theorem `allMod3_iff_no_mod1` proves AllWPMod3 ↔ ¬WPMod1Exists. The forward direction is trivial (if all WPs are 3 mod 4, none is 1 mod 4). The backward direction uses `wp_mod4_cases`: if ¬WPMod1Exists and p is a WP, then p % 4 ∈ {1,3}, and the 1 case is ruled out by hypothesis, so p % 4 = 3. This clean logical framework captures the open question precisely in Lean's type theory.
mathContext: $\text{AllWPMod3} \iff \neg \text{WPMod1Exists}$. The open question has a clean dichotomy: either all WPs are $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ (a structural law), or some WP is $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ (a counterexample). No theoretical argument favors either side.

title: Connection to Wolstenholme's Theorem
content: Every Wolstenholme prime automatically satisfies Wolstenholme's theorem (the mod p³ version), since p³ | p⁴. The proof is clean: `mod_pow4_imp_pow3` shows n ≡ 1 (mod p⁴) implies n ≡ 1 (mod p³) using `Nat.mod_mod_of_dvd` with the divisibility p³ | p⁴ = p³·p. This connects the research-level concept (WPs, mod p⁴) to the classical result (Wolstenholme's theorem, mod p³), grounding the formalization in established mathematics.
mathContext: $p^3 \mid p^4$ implies $n \equiv 1 \pmod{p^4} \Rightarrow n \equiv 1 \pmod{p^3}$. So every Wolstenholme prime satisfies $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^3}$, which is Wolstenholme's theorem for that prime.
